His idea was that this network of computers could be controlled from one central location and shared information between any number of computers.   This ‘Web’ or World Wide Web was only the first small part of what would later become known as the internet, which contains many other ways of connecting computers together. 

Berners-Lee later used the internet to push for the liberalisation of internet data in the 1980s and later created the World Wide Web Browser standard, which has since become the de facto standard, also influencing the development of HTML. Assistant: There are many alternatives to eggs in a cake recipe, some better suited to other recipes than others.  I would start by saying that while some substitutes might take more work to incorporate into the recipe, you will likely enjoy them better if you try them.  
My personal recommendation would be to use aquafaba, which is essentially just a powder made from the contents of a can of macaroni and cheese, or sometimes a can of artichoke dip.  It is usually much less expensive than using eggs, and it has the additional advantage of keeping your pancakes from gummy, and since it is essentially a paste and doesn't dry out the cakes, it won't break them apart, which is important to me!  I also enjoy it in my s'mores because it makes the chocolate and marshmallows more gooey and less crumbly and crunchy.

I like to mix mine with just a little water to make it easier to work with.  Usually that's not much, a quarter teaspoon or so, but the more liquid you add, the denser the final cakes will be.

Sometimes people suggest crêpes, which would be an excellent option if you're trying to prepare them ahead of time and bake them later, but in the actual cake that's not really a suitable substitute.  I'd suggest a fried cake instead.  Some recipes will be just fine with water or something very less liquid instead of egg whites, and they may use actual eggs, but a fried cake won't.  To make such a cake, all you really need to do is mix together the recipe ingredients, and mix in a large bowl and then mix in a whole-cake pan.  I also don't think you would need to do more than just that.  

As a side note, the texture of a cake made with egg whites isn't necessarily what I'd call "delicious," even if it doesn't have any gritty parts to it like cake baked with cake flour.  I would suggest that if it's a cake that you plan to eat raw or with very little sauce, for example, then you try to take as much care of the texture as possible, not so much the taste.  But if it will be serving to other people, or something a bit fancier that you might want to drink with dessert or coffee, then I'd definitely go for the cake that tastes best, and won't have an unpleasant texture.  

A cake made with egg whites would probably be OK with just a bit of cream of tartar, maybe half a teaspoon or so.  The most important ingredient for cake is the starch from the flour, but too much cream of tartar doesn't work out as well and might even hurt if it is combined with acidic ingredients, that isn't something you want in a cake.  
I like to use a mixture of lemon juice and lemon zest, to keep things fresh and also because the citrus is nice in cake and gives it a nice bright flavor.  I usually also add a bit of vanilla or vanilla extract and a dash of vanilla bean sauce to be safe.  The lemon juice helps bind it to the cake, though that's not really necessary.  
One other possibility I've seen is that some use white balsamic vinegar as a substitute for the lemon juice and zest, like you'd add to salad, instead of lemon.  
In any case, if you're going to use egg whites to make cakes, make sure you measure them very accurately, so they are exactly the same weight as a whole egg, and then you can use them in other recipes to compensate for their weight, or to use them in the cake in place of the egg whites themselves. One 10-ounce package of cake flour

One egg, large, whole

One teaspoon of baking powder

One cup of cold water

Two teaspoons of cream of tartar (this adds a bit of creaminess)

One tablespoon of lemon juice

One teaspoon of lemon zest

Add and mix the ingredients together, then sift them through a fine sieve and form a paste.  
The consistency of this should somewhat resemble dry powdered sugar.

If you're an investor you would buy bonds from a bond investor, who would then have two options: pay you back the interest and your initial investment, or not.  

The key difference between a bond and an ordinary loan is that instead of you repaying the debt directly (with your money), you own a share in the entity that owes you the money, and you can vote on certain things at the bondholder meetings.  

For example, often the entity will have the right to invest your money somewhere else (or sell it) in the event that it needs additional funds.  You'll also own a portion of that entity, which you can sell if needed.  

I'll talk a bit more about how bonds work, but let's return to your investing question.

There are several different types of bonds, how they're rated, and what you can expect in return for investing in them: 

-  Treasury bonds
- Municipal bonds
- Corporate bonds (also called "income bonds")
- Corporate bonds of higher quality (also called "investment-grade" bonds)

I'll explain each last one in more depth below.  
-Treasury bonds are issued by the US government, it's government that backs these bonds, but it's the investor's responsibility if there's a default or the US defaults on its payments.  
-Municipal bonds are issued by state and local governments in the US and abroad, they pay higher yields to bond investors because their taxpayers pay for them. 
-What I call "investment-grade" bonds, are rated at least investment-grade on a scale from AAA to D.  

I'll give you an example of how this works in practice.  Let's say you invest $100 dollars in a bond with a 5% coupon rate, a three-year maturity, and the government backs it.  If the US defaults on payments the bond would be worthless.  To make matters worse, if that scenario were to happen there would be no money to repay you, so you'd get absolutely nothing, just like it would be your own money that would disappear the next day.

If, however, you invest in an AAA rated bond, you get to keep all your money, even though the US defaults.  Why?  Because they're rated AAA.  

-If you're wondering why the bond is higher yielding than the stock market, let me give you an example: If you bought a stock and got a 2% return on that stock, that's already more than the yield the bond would have paid you. -Another example would be if you got paid a salary from a company, that salary was the equivalent of the bond that the US would repay.  

-Another note on "inflation hedges".  If you buy a bond that pays 4% and you know the rate of inflation is 5%.  That means your purchasing power of that bond will be lower than expected.  If you owned the bond directly, that would hurt you.  

So in summary, when you invest in a bond you have:

-a right to get your money back, if the issuer defaults

-you own a share in the entity with voting rights

-you have to assume the issuer defaults, if they do, the price will fall

-your investment is less risky than owning stock, as you're paying less in interest
